--- title: "Advanced ggplot2" subtitle: "Scientific workflows: Tools and Tips 🛠️" author: "Dr. Selina Baldauf" date: "2026-05-21" format: revealjs: footer: "Selina Baldauf // Advanced ggplot2" highlight-style: printing mainfont: Cabinet Grotesk slide-number: true show-slide-number: all incremental: true self-contained: true code-line-numbers: false theme: slides.scss auto-stretch: false editor: source execute: echo: false eval: true cache: true message: false from: markdown+emoji --- ## What is this lecture series? ### Scientific workflows: Tools and Tips :hammer_and_wrench: ::: nonincremental :date: Every 3rd Thursday :clock4: 4-5 p.m. :round_pushpin: Webex - One topic from the world of scientific workflows - Material provided [online](https://selinazitrone.github.io/tools_and_tips/) - If you don't want to miss a lecture - [Subscribe to the mailing list](https://lists.fu-berlin.de/listinfo/toolsAndTips) - For credit points: Send me a short message (Email or Webex) ::: ## Why this workshop? Default `ggplot2` plots look fine for exploration . . . ...but they're rarely publication-ready out of the box: - Default themes carry decoration you didn't ask for - Default colors aren't colorblind-safe - Text sizes don't match any output medium - Single plots — papers want A/B/C panels - Exports come out blurry or the wrong size . . . Today: a tour of the parts of the `ggplot2` ecosystem that fix these ## Plan for today ::: nonincremental 1. **Themes** — write your own and reuse it 2. **Color** — colorblind-safe palettes that stick to your groups 3. **Directing attention** — `ggtext`, `ggrepel`, `gghighlight` 4. **Multi-panel layouts** — A/B/C figures with `patchwork` 5. **Export** — get fonts and dimensions right for journals Plus a short tour of useful extension packages at the end. ::: ## Follow along ::: nonincremental Everything we do today is in this repo: [github.com/selinazitrone/advanced-ggplot-workshop](https://github.com/selinazitrone/advanced-ggplot-workshop) 1. Clone it (or download the zip) 2. Open `advanced-ggplot-workshop.Rproj` 3. From the R console: `source("install_packages.R")` For each module: I demo from `R/`, you do a short exercise from `exercises/`. ::: # Build a reusable theme {.inverse} ## The default theme carries baggage ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/plot-default-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ## A custom theme, applied ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/plot-themed-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ## Anatomy of `theme()` `theme()` controls every non-data element of the plot. Elements form an inheritance tree: ``` text ──┬── axis.text ──┬── axis.text.x │ └── axis.text.y ├── plot.title ├── plot.subtitle └── legend.text line ──┬── axis.line ──┬── axis.line.x │ └── axis.line.y ├── axis.ticks └── panel.grid ─── panel.grid.major / minor rect ──┬── plot.background └── panel.background ``` Setting a parent affects all its children. ## Cheatsheet: every theme element on one plot A beautiful reference by Henry Wang showing every named element: ::: nonincremental [henrywang.nl/ggplot2-theme-elements-demonstration](https://henrywang.nl/ggplot2-theme-elements-demonstration/) ::: . . . Keep this open while you tweak — it saves a lot of `?theme` lookups. ## Two ways to modify a theme **With `+` :** keep the base, tweak it ```r p_default + theme_minimal() + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) ``` . . . **With `%+replace%` :** start fresh, you specify everything ```r my_theme <- theme_minimal() %+replace% theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) ``` . . . Use `%+replace%` inside theme **functions** — full control, no surprises. ## Make it a function ```r theme_workshop <- function() { theme_minimal(base_size = 12) %+replace% theme( plot.title = element_text(size = 14, hjust = 0), axis.title = element_text(size = 12), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom" # ... ) } p + theme_workshop() ``` ::: nonincremental - A function composes cleanly with other layers - Easy to share, version, edit in one place ::: ## Apply globally, then source from a file Set it once at the top of a script: ```r theme_set(theme_workshop()) ``` . . . Every subsequent plot uses it — no per-plot `+ theme_workshop()`. . . . In a real project, the theme lives in its own file: ```r # at the top of every analysis script source(here::here("R", "theme_lab.R")) theme_set(theme_lab()) ``` One edit to `R/theme_lab.R` updates every figure in your project. ## Your turn :writing_hand: (8 min) ::: nonincremental Open `exercises/01_themes.R` 1. Create `R/theme_lab.R` with a function `theme_lab()`: - based on `theme_minimal()` - no minor gridlines - axis title size 12, plot title size 14 2. Source it and apply with `theme_set(theme_lab())` **Stretch goals** (if you finish early): - Custom plot background color - Google font via `sysfonts` + `showtext` - Make a second plot and confirm the theme applies automatically ::: # Color with intent {.inverse} ## Default colors carry baggage too ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/line-default-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ## With a colorblind-safe palette ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/line-okabe-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ## Pick intuitive colors when you can If a meaning is already in your reader's head, use it: ::: nonincremental - Water, sky → blue - Blood, fire → red - Vegetation → green - Gold, sun → yellow ::: . . . If there's no natural mapping, pick from a safe palette and stay consistent across all figures in the paper. ## Three safe palette families ::: nonincremental - **Okabe-Ito** — 8 hand-picked categorical colors, distinguishable for all common forms of colorblindness - **viridis** — perceptually uniform, great for continuous or many groups (`scale_*_viridis_d/c()`) - **ColorBrewer (CB-safe subset)** — qualitative, sequential, diverging palettes (`scale_*_brewer()`) ::: . . . Browse hundreds more with **`paletteer`** — a meta-package for ~2500 palettes from dozens of sources. ## Check it: `cvd_grid()` ```r library(colorblindr) cvd_grid(p) ``` Renders your plot under four simulations: ::: nonincremental - Deuteranopia (red-green) - Protanopia (red-green) - Tritanopia (blue-yellow) - Grayscale ::: . . . If you can still read the plot in all four, you're good. ## Named vectors: colors that stick **Positional** (fragile): ```r scale_color_manual(values = c("orange", "blue", "green", "navy", "red")) ``` If one continent drops out of your filtered data, every other continent shifts colors. . . . **Named** (defensive): ```r scale_color_manual(values = c( Africa = "#E69F00", Americas = "#56B4E9", Asia = "#009E73", Europe = "#0072B2", Oceania = "#D55E00" )) ``` Asia is always green, no matter which subset you plot. ## Double-coding: color + shape When you have ≤4 categories, encode the same group twice: ```r aes(color = group, shape = group) # or aes(color = group, linetype = group) ``` . . . ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/double-coding-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: Useful for colorblind viewers and for B/W print. ## Your turn :writing_hand: (8 min) ::: nonincremental Open `exercises/02_color.R` 1. Build a named Okabe-Ito vector for the 5 continents and apply with `scale_color_manual()` 2. Run `cvd_grid()` and check it survives all four simulations **Stretch goals**: - Try 2-3 other palettes from `paletteer` and check each with `cvd_grid()` — which survives best? - Make a continuous version: color points by `gdpPercap` with `scale_color_viridis_c()` ::: # Directing attention {.inverse} ## Too many lines, no story ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/asia-default-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ## `gghighlight`: dim the rest in one line ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/asia-highlight-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ```r gghighlight(country %in% c("China", "India")) ``` ## Control the highlighted colors ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/asia-colored-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ## `ggrepel`: labels at the endpoints ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/asia-labeled-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ## `ggtext`: colored words in the title ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/asia-final-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ## `annotate()`: one-off notes and arrows For a labelled event on the plot: ```r + annotate("label", x = 1960, y = 55000, label = "China's reform period\nbegan in 1978", label.size = 0, fill = "white") + annotate("segment", x = 1972, xend = 1978, y = 50000, yend = 3000, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"))) ``` ## A sprinkle: `scales` for axis labels You already saw `scales::label_dollar()` on the y-axis. The whole family is useful: ```r scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent()) scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) ``` The last renders `1200000` as `"1.2M"`. ## Your turn :writing_hand: (10 min) ::: nonincremental Open `exercises/03_attention.R` 1. Find the top 5 GDP-growth countries (1952 → 2007) and highlight them with `gghighlight`; dim the rest 2. Add `ggrepel` endpoint labels at year 2007 3. Drop the legend **Stretch goals**: - Color the 5 with a named Okabe-Ito vector - `ggtext` title naming the 5 in their colors - `annotate()` a context note ::: ## Coffee break :coffee: (5 min) # Multi-panel layouts with patchwork {.inverse} ## Three plots, named as R objects ```r p_scatter <- ggplot(...) + ... p_lines <- ggplot(...) + ... p_box <- ggplot(...) + ... ``` . . . Building plots as named objects is the small habit that unlocks composition. You'll also stop re-running long pipelines just to tweak one layer. ## Side by side, stacked, nested ```r p1 + p2 # side by side p1 / p2 # stacked p1 | p2 # alias for + (p1 + p2) / p3 # nested ``` ## Combine into A/B/C ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/patch-basic-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Collect legend and axis titles ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/patch-collect-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Tag panels automatically ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/patch-tags-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## `&` vs `+` — apply to all panels `+` modifies only the last plot in the chain. `&` applies to **every** plot: ```r (p1 + p2) / p3 + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")) ``` ## `inset_element()` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/patch-inset-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ## Your turn :writing_hand: (8 min) ::: nonincremental Open `exercises/04_patchwork.R` 1. Combine the three provided plots into an A/B/C figure with panel tags, one collected legend, shared y-axis title where it makes sense **Stretch goals**: - Compare `(p_scatter + p_lines) / p_box` vs `p_scatter / (p_lines + p_box)` — which tells the story better? - Set `widths` so `p_scatter` is twice as wide as `p_lines` - Add an `inset_element()` with a small overview plot in the corner of one panel ::: # Export for journals {.inverse} ## What you see is not what you get Default `ggsave("plot.png", p)`: - uses your IDE's plot pane dimensions - uses the system antialiaser — fuzzy text on many setups . . . What you want: ```r ggsave( "fig1.png", p, width = 89, height = 70, units = "mm", dpi = 300 ) ``` ## Real journal column widths ::: nonincremental - PLOS-Biology single column ≈ **89 mm** - PLOS-Biology double column ≈ **183 mm** - Each journal publishes its specs — check the figure guidelines ::: . . . Specify dimensions in **mm** so they match what the journal expects. ## The text-size trap A title at size 14 looks fine in your plot pane (~7 inches wide) but tiny at 89 mm. . . . Text scales with physical size, not pixel count. Iterate font sizes at the real export dimensions, not at your default pane size. ## `ggview`: preview at export size ```r library(ggview) ggview(p, width = 89, height = 70, units = "mm") ``` . . . Wraps your plot and previews it at the requested dimensions in the plot pane. No save-and-reopen cycle. ## Why `ragg::agg_png` and not plain `png()`? ```r ggsave("fig1.png", p, device = ragg::agg_png, ...) ``` ::: nonincremental - AGG renderer → better antialiasing, crisper text - Handles unicode, emoji, ligatures cleanly via `systemfonts` - Consistent across Windows / macOS / Linux ::: . . . For PDF: `device = cairo_pdf` — embeds fonts so reviewers see what you saw. ## Online vs print ::: nonincremental - Design for **print** (mm + dpi) - The PDF is the canonical format; most readers download it - Online HTML readers rescale that same image - For talks and social media, re-export at slide-deck dimensions with bigger text ::: ## Your turn :writing_hand: (5 min) ::: nonincremental Open `exercises/05_export.R` 1. Export the provided plot with default `ggsave("default.png", p)` 2. Export it with `ragg::agg_png` at PLOS single column (89 mm × 70 mm, 300 dpi) 3. Open both files, zoom in, compare the text **Stretch goals**: - Export at double-column width (183 mm) — what changes about font sizes? - Export as `cairo_pdf`; check fonts are embedded (Acrobat → Properties → Fonts) - Use `ggview()` to iterate ::: # Honorable mentions {.inverse} ## `ggdist` Halfeye, raincloud, dotsinterval. The modern bar-plot replacement. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/hm-ggdist-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: ```r ggdist::stat_halfeye(...) + geom_boxplot(...) ``` ## `ggsignif` / `ggpubr` Significance brackets and p-values on plots. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/hm-ggsignif-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ```r ggsignif::geom_signif(comparisons = list(c("Asia", "Europe"))) ``` *(Some statisticians dislike on-figure p-values — know the arguments.)* ## `ggridges` Ridgeline plots for distributions across groups or time. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/hm-ggridges-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: ```r ggridges::geom_density_ridges() ``` ## `ggh4x` Nested facets and custom strip styling for factorial designs. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/hm-ggh4x-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ```r ggh4x::facet_nested(~ continent + year) ``` ## `ggExtra` Marginal histograms / densities on a scatter. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/hm-ggmarginal-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ```r ggExtra::ggMarginal(p, type = "histogram") ``` ## `cowplot` Patchwork's older sibling. Useful helpers like `plot_grid()`, `theme_cowplot()`, `draw_plot()`. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2026_05_21_advanced_ggplot_files/figure-revealjs/hm-cowplot-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ```r cowplot::plot_grid(p1, p2, labels = c("A", "B")) ``` # Wrap up {.inverse} ## Recap ::: nonincremental The inside-out arc: 1. **Theme** — strip default decoration, define your own 2. **Color** — encode meaning, stay accessible 3. **Attention** — direct the eye where it matters 4. **Layout** — compose multi-panel figures 5. **Export** — ship at the right size and resolution ::: ## Keep learning ::: nonincremental - [Cédric Scherer's tutorials](https://www.cedricscherer.com/) — the modern ggplot2 reference - [Albert Rapp's blog](https://albert-rapp.de/) — practical, polished examples - [ggplot2 book (3rd ed)](https://ggplot2-book.org/) — the canonical reference - [R Graphics Cookbook](https://r-graphics.org/) — recipe-style problems and answers ::: ## Next lecture #### Topic t.b.a.
:date: 18th June :clock3: 4 - 5 p.m. :round_pushpin: Webex :bell: [Subscribe to the mailing list](https://lists.fu-berlin.de/listinfo/toolsAndTips) :e-mail: For topic suggestions or feedback [send me an email](mailto:selina.baldauf@fu-berlin.de) ## The end :) Questions?

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
